title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Enhance Mathematics Resources
author: Harry Zafar
summary: A secondary maths teacher explains how he uses Google Gemini to build tailored, projectable question grids with click-to-reveal answers. His central claim is that AI earns its place in the classroom only when the teacher's subject and task-design knowledge drives the prompt, because generic worksheets can never match the sequencing a specific class needs. He walks through a worked example, an 18-question grid on collecting like terms for Year 9 that starts with positive terms and builds towards higher-tier GCSE difficulty. He then gives the exact system prompt, the steps to turn Gemini Canvas output into a standalone HTML file, and fixes for common faults such as clipped questions or broken maths formatting. He is candid about limits: the model can err at A-Level, so outputs need checking. The piece is a practical, teacher-specific build guide whose real subject is the tool workflow.
points: Teacher expertise comes first: without a clear picture of a good maths activity, the prompt will produce a mediocre resource.
The main payoff is tailoring, since AI can generate questions that progress exactly as the teacher specifies, which premade worksheets cannot do.
The reusable prompt defines the grid layout, difficulty gradient, projector-friendly sizing and click-to-reveal answers, and only the topic and level change each time.
Output must be checked and iterated on: Gemini occasionally errs at A-Level and layouts need a few follow-up prompts.
The workflow needs only a Google account, a browser and Notepad, with the generated HTML saved and linked from lesson slides.
quotes: You must know what a good activity and resource for the Mathematics classroom looks like before you start using AI to generate them. Without the right prompts (which come from subject and task-design knowledge), you may end up with something that is not very good.

The most significant advantage I’ve found is that it can generate questions specifically tailored to my class, in a way that premade worksheets can’t, and that would take me a long time to make myself.
AI can be wrong. I’ve found it to occasionally make mistakes with A-Level Maths so far, so watch out for this. I’ve never seen it make mistakes in KS3 or GCSE-level Maths.

I use Gemini most often to generate sets of questions for students to complete, in a format suitable for display (projecting) on the board. I find this advantageous for learners in my classroom because I can specify exactly how I want questions to progress and ensure learners focus on the specific skill I intend.
A key point here is that the more specific you are, the better output you will get. You could write 2 pages of information, if you like.

It will occasionally do things like cut off questions from the screen, or have text that is too small. It might take a few prompts to resolve all these issues. Just describe the issue for Gemini to fix. This can take a bit of time, but overall, I find it saves far more time than writing the questions yourself.
